tagline: A castle, a prince, and the Rhine
overview:
Liechtenstein is one of the smallest countries on Earth, a sliver of Alpine valley and mountainside squeezed between Switzerland and Austria. At just 160 square kilometers it is smaller than Washington, D.C., and a fit walker can cross it in a day. The capital, Vaduz, is a small town on the Rhine River overlooked by a medieval castle where the prince and his family actually live. The country has no airport, no highway, and no army, yet it is one of the richest nations in the world per person.

About 40,000 people live in Liechtenstein, speaking German and an Alemannic dialect close to Swiss German. It is a constitutional monarchy where the prince holds real power, including the right to veto laws, alongside an elected parliament of 25 members. Liechtenstein has close ties with Switzerland, using the Swiss franc and sharing open borders. Its economy runs on banking and, surprisingly, industry: tiny Liechtenstein makes dental products, power tools, and machine parts sold worldwide, and it has more registered companies than citizens.
landAndNature: The Rhine River forms the entire western border, flowing through a flat valley floor where the villages and farms lie. From there the land climbs steeply into the Rätikon range of the Alps, with Grauspitz the highest point at 2,599 meters. The mountain villages of Malbun and Steg sit in a high side valley, where skiing draws visitors in winter and hikers in summer, and where the Sareis chairlift and the trail of the Fürstensteig cling to cliffs. About 40 percent of the country is forest. Chamois, ibex, marmots, and red deer live on the slopes, and golden eagles hunt overhead. Winters are cold and snowy in the mountains but mild in the valley thanks to the warm föhn wind that blows down from the Alps.
peopleAndCulture: Life in Liechtenstein is quiet, prosperous, and closely tied to its neighbors, with many people commuting in from Switzerland and Austria for work each day. Most citizens are Roman Catholic. Food is Alpine and hearty: käsknöpfle, small cheese dumplings with fried onions and applesauce, and ribel, a cornmeal dish once eaten by farmers, are national favorites. On National Day, August 15, the prince invites the entire population to a reception in the castle gardens, followed by fireworks over Vaduz. Skiing is the top sport, and the country has won all its Olympic medals in Alpine skiing, more per person than any nation. Liechtenstein is also famous among collectors for its beautiful postage stamps, which once brought in a large share of the national income.
history: Romans built a road through the Rhine valley, and Alemannic tribes settled here in the 400s. In the Middle Ages the lands of Vaduz and Schellenberg were small lordships within the Holy Roman Empire. In 1699 and 1712 the wealthy Liechtenstein family of Vienna bought them so they could have a seat in the imperial assembly, and in 1719 the emperor made them the Principality of Liechtenstein. For 200 years the princes barely visited. The country stayed neutral in both world wars and abolished its army in 1868. After World War I it turned from Austria toward Switzerland, adopting the Swiss franc in 1924. Prince Franz Josef II became the first prince to live in Vaduz Castle in 1938. Women gained the right to vote only in 1984, and Liechtenstein joined the United Nations in 1990.
funFacts: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are the world's only doubly landlocked countries, surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries.
The country's army was disbanded in 1868; legend says the last 80 soldiers came home from a war with 81 men, having made a friend.
Liechtenstein has won ten Olympic medals, all in Alpine skiing, more per person than any other country.
In 2011 Liechtenstein offered itself for rent to groups for about 70,000 dollars a night, complete with a symbolic key and custom street signs.
The prince invites every citizen to his castle garden for drinks each year on National Day, August 15.
